description: We are a team of passionate engineering students interested in space exploration, AI, data visualization, and software development. Our goal is to build an interactive lunar mission planning tool using NASA data to help compare landing sites, analyze illumination, assess communication opportunities, and support mission planning.
summary:
Project Golden Dawns – CLPS Lunar Mission Browser

Project Golden Dawns aims to simplify lunar landing site analysis by developing an interactive web-based Lunar Mission Browser. Missions to the Moon's south pole face significant challenges due to extreme lighting conditions and limited communication opportunities with Earth. Understanding sunlight availability and Earth visibility is essential for selecting suitable landing locations and planning successful lunar missions.

Our project provides an intuitive platform that allows users to explore and compare potential lunar landing sites and dates through interactive visualizations. It focuses on displaying the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon, helping users understand solar illumination conditions, power generation potential, and direct-to-Earth communication windows.

By presenting complex lunar mission information in a clear, accessible, and interactive format, Project Golden Dawns aims to make lunar mission planning easier for researchers, educators, students, and space enthusiasts while supporting future lunar exploration.
details:
CLPS Lunar Mission Browser — Implementation Plan

An interactive lunar south pole mission planning and educational observatory that computes Sun and Earth visibility, local terrain horizon masking, power potential, and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows across candidate NASA Artemis and CLPS landing sites.

---

User Review & Critical Decisions

> \[!IMPORTANT]

> All core architectural and product decisions from our discovery round are locked in below. Review and approve to begin full end-to-end implementation.

Confirmed Runtime Strategy: Deliver a live, self-contained TypeScript + Express + React web application on port 3000 (for instant zero-setup browser execution in the preview) alongside the complete Python 3.11 + FastAPI + NAIF SPICE backend, JPL Horizons verification suite, kernel fetcher, and Docker Compose bundle.

Confirmed Scope: Implement all 8 build stages end-to-end—ephemeris math, computed metrics & windows, interactive south pole site map, Timeline & Elevation charts, Comparison & Radar views, LOLA terrain horizon masking, 3D Sky Dome & 2D Polar views, Landing Date Finder heatmap, Simple/Expert modes, Educator guided lessons, Validation dashboard, and CSV/JSON/PNG/PDF exports.

Confirmed Map & Horizon Data: Combine NASA Moon Trek WMTS south polar LRO LOLA hillshade tiles (with a deterministic procedural LOLA relief canvas fallback) with precomputed 360° (1° bin) horizon elevation profiles for the 7 NASA preset sites and on-demand lunar-curvature ray-marching for custom coordinates.

Confirmed Default Mode & Theme: Open in Dark Mission Control aesthetic with Simple Mode active by default for immediate plain-English clarity ("Is it sunny? Can it see Earth?"), with a single-click toggle into Expert Mode for full orbital, antenna-margin, power-model, and terrain controls.

---

1. Overview & Core Concept

What It Does: Mission planners, students, and the public pick up to 5 lunar landing sites (focusing on the South Pole) and a date range, immediately seeing when the Sun illuminates solar arrays, when Earth clears the local terrain for Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communications, when both occur simultaneously, and which landing dates maximize mission uptime.

Target Audiences:

Mission Planners (Expert Mode): High-precision azimuth/elevation series, configurable DTE antenna mask margins, vertical-tracking vs. horizontal solar power curves, longest continuous eclipse & comm-blackout metrics, sortable multi-site comparison, and CSV/JSON/PNG/PDF exports.

Educators & Students (Educator Mode): Interactive guided tour plus three hands-on lessons ("Why is the south pole always twilight?", "Why does Earth wobble in the lunar sky?", "Choose the best landing site").

General Public (Simple Mode): Plain-English daily status answers, clear visual sky dome, and an accessible bottom Explain tray translating orbital mechanics into everyday language.

Key Value: First mission insight within 3 clicks (Pick Site → Pick Dates → Inspect Timeline & Sky Dome), sub-second cached response times, and shareable URLs encoding the entire mission state.

---

2. User Experience & Visual Design

Key User Flows:

3-Click Discovery (Zero-State to Insight): App loads with Shackleton Crater Rim and a 14-day mission window pre-selected so the Timeline, Sky Dome, and Plain-English Explain bar populate immediately. Users click any preset or tap the South Pole Map to add up to 5 color-coded sites, adjust the date range/step or scrub the time slider, and switch visualization tabs.

Simple ↔ Expert Switching: In Simple Mode, technical knobs (horizon ray-marching math, antenna margin, panel cosine incidence) stay tucked away while plain-language summaries and tooltips explain azimuth, elevation, libration, horizon mask, and DTE. Switching to Expert Mode reveals the full mission engineering controls, power wattage curves, and tabular diagnostics.

Landing Date Optimization: Selecting a 14-day (or custom) mission duration and opening the Landing Date Finder displays a year-long heatmap of simultaneous Sun + Earth visibility score; clicking any cell snaps the entire workspace to that landing window.

Verification & Learning: Switching to Validation inspects side-by-side accuracy checks against JPL Horizons (`< 0.05°` tolerance) and polar libration/solar-altitude bounds; clicking Lessons launches the interactive Educator Mode tour.

Visual Identity & Theme (Science & Space Telemetry):

Aesthetic Direction: Calibrated dark aerospace mission console—flat obsidian surfaces, crisp `1px` hairline structural borders, zero decorative blur/glow clutter, and rigorous tabular numerals.

Color Palette & Tokens:

`--bg-canvas` (`#07090E`): 60% deep-space primary background.

`--bg-surface` (`#0F172A`) & `--border-hairline` (`#1E293B`): 30% flat structural panels and coordinate grids.

Semantic Telemetry Accents (10% budget, color-blind-safe with paired glyphs/patterns): Solar Sunlit (`#F59E0B` Amber + hatch/sun glyph), Earth DTE (`#06B6D4` Cyan + signal glyph), Simultaneous Both (`#10B981` Emerald + check glyph), Shadow/Blackout (`#475569` Slate + diagonal stripe).

Typography & Hierarchy: `Plus Jakarta Sans` for crisp UI headings and plain-English explanations paired with `IBM Plex Mono` (`font-mono tabular-nums`) for all coordinates, timestamps, azimuth/elevation readouts, and comparison tables.

Layout Architecture:

Top Header (3-Zone Contract): Brand wordmark (`CLPS Lunar Mission Browser`), single-line workspace navigation links (Workspace, Compare, Date Finder, Validation, Lessons), and primary action button (Share Link).

Workspace Control Ribbon: Houses the `Simple | Expert` segmented toggle, active mission summary, Guided Tour trigger, and Export menu (`CSV`, `JSON`, `Chart PNG`, `PDF Summary`).

Asymmetric Split Console: Fixed left Plan column (South Pole Map + 7 verified presets + custom lat/lon, date/step controls, time playback slider, and Expert settings) beside the primary visualization stage (`Sky View`, `Timeline`, `Elevation Charts`, `Compare`, `Landing Date Finder`) and the bottom Explain / telemetry summary tray.

Interactive Feedback & Accessibility:

Instant loading skeletons during multi-month or year-sweep computations, inline validation banners for out-of-range coordinates or date spans, keyboard-accessible tabs/sliders, WCAG AA contrast, and pattern+label encoding on Gantt timelines so no state relies solely on hue.

---

3. Key Product Decisions & Trade-Offs

Decision 1: Dual Ephemeris Engine (TypeScript Live Engine + Python SPICE Reference Backend)

Chosen Approach: Implement a full analytical lunar ephemeris in TypeScript inside the Node/Express server for the live preview (`MOON\_ME` body-fixed vectors, topocentric ENU conversion, solar disk angular integration `0.267°`, optical+physical libration) while providing the complete Python 3.11 + FastAPI + `spiceypy` (`naif0012.tls`, `de440s.bsp`, `pck00011.tpc`, `moon\_pa\_de440\_200625.bpc`, `moon\_de440\_250416.tf`) + `skyfield` fallback backend, `pytest` Horizons validation suite, and Docker Compose setup.

Why: The AI Studio runtime runs Node.js on port 3000; computing ephemeris natively in Express guarantees the web app runs interactively out of the box without requiring users to download 100+ MB SPICE kernels first, while the Python package fulfills exact NASA SPICE production deployment.

Alternatives Considered: Python-only backend (would fail to boot in the Node preview environment).

Decision 2: Precomputed LOLA Profiles + On-Demand Analytic South Pole DEM + Moon Trek WMTS

Chosen Approach: Load verified NASA/Artemis III coordinates for the 7 preset sites (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache Rim, Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim, Haworth, Leibnitz Beta Plateau / Mons Mouton) with precomputed 360° horizon profiles, render NASA Moon Trek South Pole WMTS tiles on an interactive polar stereographic canvas (with a deterministic procedural LOLA hillshade fallback if offline/CORS-blocked), and compute custom-site 150 km ray-marched terrain horizons on demand using a calibrated LOLA south-polar elevation model in TS (and GeoTIFF rasterio ray-marching in Python).

Why: Avoids multi-gigabyte GeoTIFF downloads during preview startup while still delivering genuine azimuth-dependent terrain masking and lunar curvature physics (`d^2 / 2R`).

Decision 3: Custom Lightweight WebGL2 Three.js Sky Dome + Plotly.js Scientific Charts

Chosen Approach: Build the 3D Sky Dome using vanilla `three` (`WebGLRenderer` inside an isolated `useRef` container with software-WebGL detection, `OrbitControls`, `SRGBColorSpace`, horizon terrain silhouette ring, and Sun/Earth orbital arcs) paired with a 2D Polar Azimuth/Elevation toggle, and render Timeline, Elevation, Radar, and Heatmap charts with `plotly.js` (`react-plotly.js` / direct `Plotly.newPlot`) for built-in hover crosshairs and PNG export.

Why: Direct `three` lifecycle management avoids React 19 peer-dependency conflicts with `react-three-fiber` while guaranteeing rock-solid rendering on both hardware GPUs and headless software WebGL.

Decision 4: URL-Encoded State + Server-Side Caching

Chosen Approach: Synchronize active sites, date range, step size, horizon mode, Earth margin, panel type, and Simple/Expert mode into URL query parameters, backed by an in-memory + persistent cache keyed by `(site, start, end, step, horizon\_mode)`.

Why: Makes every mission scenario instantly shareable via a single click and ensures `< 2s` (sub-100ms cached) responses.

---

4. Technical Architecture & Data Strategy

Data Model & Core Computations:

Site: `{ id, name, lat, lon, heightKm, color, sourceNote, isPreset }`

TimeStepSample: `{ timestampIso, sunAzDeg, sunElDeg, sunVisibleFraction, earthAzDeg, earthElDeg, earthVisible, horizonSunElDeg, horizonEarthElDeg, bothVisible, powerFactor }`

VisibilityWindow: `{ type: 'sun' | 'earth' | 'both', startIso, endIso, durationHours }`

SiteMetrics: `{ sunlitAnyPct, sunlitHalfPct, sunlitFullPct, earthVisiblePct, bothVisiblePct, longestDarknessHours, longestEarthBlackoutHours, avgPowerFraction, windows\[] }`

HorizonProfile: `360` azimuth bins (`0°..359°`, clockwise from North) giving terrain elevation angle in degrees including lunar curvature correction `arctan((h\_target - h\_obs) / d - d / (2 \* R\_moon))`.

Interactive Component & State Mapping:

Site Picker & Map: Clicking the Moon Trek South Pole stereographic canvas converts `(x, y)` pixel coordinates to `(lat, lon)` via inverse south polar stereographic projection and appends a custom site (up to 5 max, each assigned a distinct color-blind-safe palette slot). Selecting any of the 7 verified presets or editing lat/lon triggers validation (`-90 <= lat <= 90`, `-180 <= lon <= 360`) and fires `POST /api/compute`.

Time Slider & Playback: Scrubbing or pressing Play/Pause advances the active timestamp index across all open views, moving the Sun and Earth spheres along their orbital path arcs in the 3D Sky Dome and updating the live readout and crosshair marker on Elevation & Timeline charts.

Compare & Export: Sorting the metrics table reorders sites and updates the Plotly Radar trace; Export triggers CSV/JSON downloads from `/api/export`, PNG capture of active Plotly/Three.js canvases, or a clean formatted one-page mission brief PDF via print-optimized report layout.

Landing Date Finder: Clicking "Sweep Year" computes rolling mission-duration windows (default 14 days) across 365 days per selected site and renders an interactive heatmap; clicking any date cell updates `start`/`end` and switches back to the Timeline.

Educator Mode & Validation: Toggling Lessons opens an interactive step-by-step tour that loads real lunar south pole scenarios (e.g., comparing Shackleton Rim vs. Malapert Massif to demonstrate Earth libration and polar twilight). Opening Validation displays live ephemeris output against archived JPL Horizons reference points across 3 sites × 5 epochs alongside polar bounds checks.
